NICE stock raises 2026 EPS outlook after third-quarter beat
sum: NICE reported stronger-than-guided third-quarter results on November 4, 2026, and raised its full-year adjusted earnings outlook. The company said in its November 4 press release that revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share exceeded the high end of guidance.

Third-quarter revenue rose 8.0 percent year over year to 790.7 million US dollars. Cloud revenue increased 10.6 percent, while the company said growth would have been 12.2 percent excluding an atypical 10 million US dollar customer credit.

AI annual recurring revenue climbed 46 percent year over year to 392 million US dollars, equal to 16 percent of cloud revenue. International revenue increased 33 percent, highlighting areas of demand as NICE continues to position its platform around customer-experience artificial intelligence.

The reported results also showed pressure on profitability. GAAP operating income fell to 120.6 million US dollars from 160.8 million US dollars a year earlier, while non-GAAP operating margin declined to 27.0 percent from 31.5 percent. Non-GAAP diluted earnings per share came in at 2.84 US dollars, compared with 3.18 US dollars in the prior-year quarter.

NICE reiterated full-year 2026 non-GAAP revenue guidance of 3.17 billion to 3.19 billion US dollars and raised its adjusted diluted EPS outlook to 11.12 to 11.32 US dollars. The guidance includes expected cloud-revenue growth of approximately 12 percent.

Management also plans to reduce the global workforce by approximately 5 percent while cutting management layers and expanding partner-led delivery. NICE expects pre-tax restructuring charges of 15 million to 20 million US dollars, primarily in the fourth quarter; these charges will be excluded from non-GAAP results.

Loudoun County official shares data center lessons as Washington County uses moratorium to study its options
sum: Loudoun County, Virginia, has spent more than two decades as the world’s data center hub. On Oct. 30, one of its top officials told members of the Greater Hagerstown Committee what that growth has delivered and what it has cost.

Joe Kroboth, Loudoun’s deputy county administrator, presented “Data Centers: The Loudoun County Experience” as Washington County works through a 12-month moratorium on data center applications. Kroboth previously served as Washington County’s public works director while Greater Hagerstown Committee Executive Director Jim Kercheval was a county commissioner.

“We’ve been wanting to try to find a nice, unbiased, neutral source to come in and just talk to us about data centers,” Kercheval said in an interview on NewsTalk 103.7 FM. “What’s the good, what’s the bad? What’s the challenges?”

Kroboth said Loudoun has 233 data centers that are operating or under construction, supporting about 17,000 jobs on roughly 3 percent of the county’s land. The county projects $1.3 billion in data center revenue for fiscal 2027, about 40 percent of its budget. Its real property tax rate has fallen from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to 80.5 cents.

Kercheval said the revenue has also helped Loudoun pay for roads and other infrastructure. Jobs are a smaller part of the picture. Kroboth said a typical data center employs 20 to 50 people, although outside trades and support work add to that number.

Kroboth also described the problems that have filled Loudoun’s public hearings. He called noise the top complaint and said the biggest issue is electrical transmission, because large projects need high-voltage lines and substations that may run near homes.

He said Washington County has one 500,000-volt line, with its other transmission lines carrying 138,000 volts. He advised local officials to determine how a large project would receive power before one is proposed, and to address data centers in the comprehensive plan and zoning rules.

sum: BRONX (WABC) -- Bronx artist Devon Rodriguez built a worldwide following by doing what he had been doing since childhood: drawing.

Long before his work attracted attention on social media, Rodriguez said art provided an escape from a difficult childhood in the Bronx, a story he now chronicles in his new memoir, "Work in Progress."

"Growing up in the Bronx, I was always around a lot of shady people, you know, my mom was very abusive and then my dad abandoned me and, you know, I had all these bad influences. I was almost like a little adult, I would have to wake up 8, 9 years old and my mom is like crashed out from the night before. And I just have to go to school by myself. There was no breakfast," Rodriguez said.
Rodriguez said his grandmother spent years trying to get him out of the home.
"She always used to try to get me to tell the school so I could be removed from my home. Growing up in the Bronx, I was always like, nah I'm not a snitch," he said.
"I was always, always drawing. There was nothing else I wanted to do," he said.
Rodriguez applied to an art high school in Manhattan but did not get in, instead attending his zone school in the Bronx. There, he said his art teachers had a profound impact on his life.

We're upgrading our rating on Wells Fargo as the stock's pullback offers a nice entry point
sum: Wells Fargo shares dipped 2% Tuesday after the bank reported mixed third-quarter results. However, we think better days are ahead as management's efforts to improve returns take hold, and we're upgrading the stock as a result. Total revenue at the bank increased 2% year over year to $21.9 billion in the third quarter, missing the LSEG-compiled consensus estimate of $22.3 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) for the three months ending Sept. 30 rose 13% to $1.87, beating the $1.85 consensus estimate. Bottom line We're not surprised to see a bit of weakness on Tuesday due to misses on key operating lines. Revenue missed expectations by $430 million, with shortfalls from both net interest income (NII) and non-interest income, a collection of Wells' fee-based businesses. Non-interest expenses came in below expectations, which is encouraging, but the $112 million beat versus the FactSet consensus didn't make up for all of the top-line softness. Given the bank's sensitivity to interest rates, we should start to see NII trend higher in this higher-rate environment. Net interest margin (NIM) — a key measure of a profitability, measuring the spread between what a bank earns on loans and pays out on deposits — stabilized quarter over quarter at 2.43%. This is in keeping with what CFO Michael Santomassimo said at a Barclays conference last month . The stabilization was a big deal because it ended four straight quarters of sequential declines, and the trend is expected to continue into the fourth quarter. It also beat expectations of 2.41%, which is notable because the bank entered today with misses in nine of the past 10 quarters. The bank said the better-than-expected performance was driven by slightly higher cash and securities balances, slightly lower funding costs, and additional efficiency in the deployment of its markets balance sheet. For Wells, a lot of attention is placed on NII and how the bank's NIM performs relative to the yield curve. However, we do not think investors should ignore the progress being made in building out a competitive investment bank — a big priority for CEO Charlie Scharf.

sum: While President Donald Trump's war with the networks dominates the headlines, a far more consequential fight is unfolding in a Lower Manhattan courthouse. At stake? The economics of journalism itself, and the war is sparking options traders' interest.

On Friday, newly unsealed statements from Microsoft and OpenAI executives threatened the "fair-use" defense in the New York Times lawsuit. The defense rests on showing that the accused product is neither a substitute for nor a direct competitor to the source work.

According to the unsealed material, an OpenAI executive allegedly acknowledged their chatbots were exactly that: an "existential threat" to journalism, delivering the information directly and sparing the reader the click-through, per the Wall Street Journal.

OpenAI allegedly copied millions of copyrighted articles for training, possibly exploiting hacks to retrieve them, and Microsoft's own director of applied science, Brent Hecht, reportedly described the training as "the largest theft of labor in human history," according to the Washington Post, while the companies' own data showed Times' click-through rates dropping precipitously.

OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, meanwhile, reportedly wrote in 2017 that he was "deeply motivated by the gazillions" he hoped to earn commercializing the technology, according to the Financial Times, and allegedly replied "ah nice" when told an employee had found a hack around the Times' paywall.

These findings meaningfully raise the odds of either a massive settlement and licensing deal or, failing that, a Times victory at trial that would be catastrophic for the defendants and enormously remunerative for the plaintiff.

The one wrinkle for the Times was the September 1st statement of interest from the Department of Justice asking the court to hold that training AI models on copyrighted work is fair use, citing national security. If foreign adversaries will train on anything they can access by any means, the argument goes, restricting U.S. systems risks ceding an insurmountable lead.

Ex-Guns N’ Roses Drummer Frank Ferrer Shares What People Get Wrong About Axl Rose
sum: Ex-Guns N' Roses drummer Frank Ferrer recently shared what he thinks people get wrong about Axl Rose in his first interview since parting ways with the band last year.

Guns announced Ferrer's "amicable" departure in March of 2025 and revealed Isaac Carpenter as their new drummer the very next day. More than a year later, Ferrer has opened up on his time with the band, his split and more during a conversation with Rolling Stone.
After working with Rose for nearly two decades, the drummer explained what he thinks people get wrong about the vocalist.

"[People misunderstand] that he’s a mean guy. I think the world thinks that he’s a scary, mean guy. And he’s the complete opposite. He doesn’t suffer fools, so that might piss people off. But he’s generous and super funny and worried about us all the time, worried about, 'Hey, you guys, how you guys doing?' 'Hey, is Frank okay? Hey Frank, are you okay?'" Ferrer said.

"It’s that kind of stuff constantly. I wish they could know him the way I know him. That’s the only way I could say it. He’s a great musician, great singer, all that stuff that goes in the pot, but he’s a good man."

Ferrer went on to praise Rose for "busting his ass" and trying to deliver the best he possibly can every time he steps on the stage. He added that whenever someone in the band isn't feeling their best, hearing Rose sing and push himself inspires them to give it their all too.
During the interview, Ferrer also shared a bit about his earliest interactions with the singer when he first joined the band. He recalled that Rose was "super nice and friendly."
